newsitem.title: GERMANY: Private banks urge EU to block Bonn bank move.
newsitem.headline: Private banks urge EU to block Bonn bank move.

text.p: Germany's private sector banks on Monday appealed to European Union nations to block a move by the Bonn government to enshrine state protection for public sector banks in European Union law.

The Federal Association of German Banks, which represents private sector banks, said Bonn's application to allow state guarantees in an amendment to the Maastricht Treaty was an "unbelievable process" which would promote unfair competition.

"It must not succeed, it would be a catastrophe for Europe's single market because the basis for the single market is to have equal competition," Karl-Heinz Boos, managing director of the association, told Reuters.
Boos said Bonn filed an application on May 28 to have the protection included in the Maastricht II Treaty to be agreed at an EU summit in Amsterdam in mid-June.
He said Bonn's move would make it less likely that the EU Commission would investigate public banks for allegedly receiving subsidies in the form of cheap state capital.

The Commission is unlikely to act before it sees how the German proposal is received at the Amsterdam conference. The Commission's reluctance to intervene is also well known as the issue is highly political, analysts said.

The dispute dates back to a complaint filed by the private banks with the EU Commission in 1994 over allegations that 11 billion marks ($6.4 billion) of state capital transferred to publicly-owned regional banks, or Landesbanken, since 1990 constituted a breach of EU subsidy rules.

The banks have failed to reach agreement despite mediation by the German government, which is believed to be anxious to avoid an EU investigation which could call Germany's giant public sector banking system into question.

The Landesbanken are owned by their respective federal states and savings bank associations. They do not offer retail banking but compete with private banks in corporate finance, securities trading and issuing.
But Friedel Neuber, head of the biggest Landesbank, Westdeutsche Landesbank, and president of the Federal Association of Public Banks, has repeatedly denied that the public banks are at an advantage.

Neuber recently caused a stir by saying the more than 600 savings banks, seen as crucial to persuading a sceptical German public to accept the euro currency, would be more critical of monetary union if the public banking system were called into question.

The federal states in 1990 started integrating their regional housing development agencies into the regional banks to beef up the banks' weak equity capital before tougher EU rules on capital adequacy came into force in 1993.
WestLB alone received four billion marks in fresh equity capital by integrating North Rhine-Westphalia's housing development agency in 1992.
The private banks see this as distorting competition because it enabled the regional banks to obtain capital at a far lower price than would be charged for funds in the private sector.

Separately Martin Kohlhaussen, chief executive of Germany's third-largest private sector bank, Commerzbank, said that all the private banks wanted was a level playing field and that he hoped Brussels would soon make a decision.
